changes.new: The kingdom of Kartli, in what is now eastern Georgia, became Christian in the fourth century. It came through the preaching of a woman the tradition calls Nino. Kartli then held on to that faith for three centuries, on a frontier where Persia had every reason to prise it loose. Its oldest surviving book, written in the 470s or 480s, tells the story of Shushanik. She was an Armenian princess married to the local ruler. He left Christianity for Zoroastrianism, and when she would not follow him, he locked her up and beat her until she died. Georgia built its own alphabet, its own monasteries, and an unusually rich life of worship. Georgian manuscripts keep the worship of fifth- to eighth-century Jerusalem more fully than any Greek source does. Around 609, at the third council of Dvin, its church broke with Armenia and took the Chalcedonian side. That is why the two neighboring churches of the Caucasus have belonged to different communions ever since.

S6: he abandoned Christianity for Zoroastrianism; imprisoned ('locked her up') and beat her until she died rather than follow him. S7: own alphabet, monasteries, unusually rich liturgical life ('life of worship'). S8: manuscripts preserve fifth- to eighth-century Jerusalem worship more fully than any Greek source. S9: 'Around 609', third council of Dvin, break with Armenia, Chalcedonian side. S10: two neighboring Caucasian churches in different communions since. Nothing added.

changes.new: The Georgian Orthodox Church that came out of this is still the church of Georgia. The same body has carried on through the centuries of medieval revival to the present. Its choice around 609 set it for good in the Eastern Orthodox family, and not with its Armenian neighbor. Its greatest gift to everyone else came almost by accident. Georgian scribes translated and kept the books of worship used in Jerusalem. So scholars can now work out how the holy city really worshipped in late antiquity, and they do it largely from Georgian manuscripts. And churches built at the very end of this period, like Jvari above Mtskheta, still stand almost as they were.

changes.new: Beside Armenia and Georgia there was a third Christian kingdom in the Caucasus. This was Albania, in what is now Azerbaijan and the south of Dagestan. It had its own royal line, its own bishops and its own alphabet. In the late fifth century it held a council at Aghuen. The council made rules for the clergy and for marriage, and set out what the nobles owed the church. Albania also produced a history, put together from older material by a writer known as Movses Daskhurantsi. That is very nearly all the story it left. It was pressed between Persian, Byzantine and then Arab power, and between the rival loyalties of its Armenian and Georgian neighbors. In 705 it lost its independent standing, when its catholicos was placed under the Armenian church. Its written language was all but lost for more than a thousand years. Then, in 1996, palimpsests at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Sinai were found to hold Caucasian Albanian scripture. The pages had been scraped and written over with later Georgian text.

changes.new: No church carries on under this name. After 705 its catholicos had to answer to the Armenian church. But the see itself lived on inside that church, and a new catholicos of Albania took office around 1701. Over the centuries its people merged with the Armenians, and the see was done away with early in the nineteenth century. The Udi people of Azerbaijan are generally seen as descended from its Christians. Its most striking survival stayed hidden until recently. In 1996, palimpsests at Sinai were found to keep its alphabet and its scripture. With them, scholars have begun to rebuild a language and a way of worship. For over a thousand years, nobody had been able to read them.

changes.new: Benedict of Nursia left Rome for a cave at Subiaco. Around 529 he ended up founding a monastery on the hill of Monte Cassino. Italy was being torn apart, first by the Gothic wars and then by the Lombard invasions. What he left behind was a rule: seventy-three short chapters on prayer, work, sleep, food, guests, discipline and the election of an abbot. Much of it, most scholars now think, was drawn from an older and harsher text, the anonymous Rule of the Master. Benedict cut it down and softened it, with an eye for what ordinary people could actually keep up. A generation later Gregory the Great, a monk before he was a pope, wrote the only account we have of Benedict's life. He also governed the Italian church through more than 850 letters, which show the same world from the other side. They tell of famine, plague, refugees, Lombard armies, and the daily running of a church trying to hold itself together.

Nothing added.

changes.new: The Rule became the standard for monks in the West. Carolingian reformers made it the norm across the Frankish empire. It stands behind the Cluniacs, the Cistercians and the Benedictine congregations that keep it today. Its language of stability, obedience and moderation reached far beyond the cloister. So did the way it built the day around fixed hours of prayer, and both passed into the West's habits of work and time. Monte Cassino itself was destroyed again and again — by Lombards, by Saracens, by earthquake, and by Allied bombing in 1944 — and rebuilt every time. Monks live there now.

His letters also tell us about the early English church, the Frankish church of Gaul and the imperial church at Constantinople.

changes.new: The Rome Gregory was born into around 540 had been besieged, taken, retaken and emptied within living memory. The Gothic wars and Justinian's reconquest had wrecked the city and the countryside that fed it. From 568 the Lombards held most of the peninsula. The imperial government sat at Ravenna and had little left to spend on Rome. Gregory was city prefect and gave it up. He turned the family house on the Caelian into a monastery, and was sent to Constantinople as the pope's representative. He was elected bishop in 590, during a plague, and spent fourteen years doing a job that had quietly become something else. The letters show what it was. He ran the papal estates in Sicily as the city's food supply and audited the men who managed them. He paid soldiers and bargained with Lombard dukes when the exarch would not. He ransomed prisoners. He told bishops in Gaul, Spain, Africa and Illyricum what he thought they were doing wrong, at length. He refused the title of universal bishop when Constantinople's patriarch used it. He already called himself servant of the servants of God, a title Pope Damasus and Augustine had used before him. In 596 he sent a party of his own monks to Kent. Then he wrote to them again and again about what to do with pagan temples, and how far to insist on Roman custom. The Pastoral Rule, written at the start of all this, is the book underneath the rest. It argues that the government of souls is the art of arts, and that different people must be told the same truth in different ways. And it holds that to want the office is already to be unfit for it.

changes.new: The Pastoral Rule became the standard book on the bishop's office in the West, and it stayed in use for a thousand years. Carolingian councils ruled that bishops should own it and read it. Alfred had it translated into English, meaning, he said, to send a copy to every bishop in his kingdom. The mission to Kent is why there is an English church in communion with Rome at all. It is also why the early English church has a Roman half. Then there is the working model of the bishop of Rome as the practical government of central Italy. He fed the city from church estates, dealt with invaders and paid troops. That is where the temporal power of the papacy really begins, whatever later documents claimed for it.
